grammar.title: Reported speech: statements, questions and commands
grammar.summary: When we report what someone said, we usually move the verb one tense back (am → was, will → would) and change pronouns and time words. Reported questions use normal statement word order, and commands use tell/ask + person + (not) to + verb.
grammar.summaryMn: Бусдын хэлсэн үгийг дамжуулахдаа ихэвчлэн үйл үгийн цагийг нэг алхам ухрааж (am → was, will → would), төлөөний үг болон цаг хугацааны үгсийг өөрчилнө. Дамжуулсан асуулт энгийн хүүрнэх өгүүлбэрийн үгийн дараалалтай байна. Тушаал, хүсэлтийг tell/ask + хүн + (not) to + үйл үг хэлбэрээр дамжуулна.
structure: Statements: say (that) + clause · tell + person + (that) + clause → 'I'm tired.' → She said (that) she was tired.

Tense changes (one step back): am/is → was · are → were · present simple → past simple · present continuous → past continuous · present perfect / past simple → past perfect · will → would · can → could · must / have to → had to
Yes/no questions: ask (+ person) + if/whether + subject + verb → 'Are you OK?' → He asked (me) if I was OK.
Wh- questions: ask (+ person) + question word + subject + verb → 'Where do you live?' → She asked (me) where I lived.
Commands and requests: tell/ask + person + (not) to + verb → 'Don't be late.' → He told me not to be late.
Time and place words: today → that day · tomorrow → the next day · yesterday → the day before · now → then · here → there · this → that

usage.example: Ana said she was working from home that day.
usage.useMn: Хэн нэгний өмнө нь хэлсэн зүйлийг дамжуулах

usage.use: Report yes/no questions with if or whether
usage.example: My manager asked me whether I had finished the report.
usage.useMn: Тийм/үгүй асуултыг if эсвэл whether ашиглан дамжуулах

usage.use: Report wh- questions with the question word + statement word order
usage.example: The journalist asked her why she had deleted her account.
usage.useMn: Асуух үгтэй асуултыг асуух үг + хүүрнэх өгүүлбэрийн дараалалаар дамжуулах

usage.example: The doctor told me to rest for a few days.

usage.use: Keep the tense when the reporting verb is in the present, or when the information is still true
usage.example: He says he's running late. / She told me she lives in Berlin.
usage.useMn: Үйл үг нь одоо цагт (says) байвал эсвэл мэдээлэл одоо ч үнэн бол цагийг өөрчлөхгүй байж болно

examples.note: No 'does' in the reported question; statement word order; no question mark.

pairs.why: In a reported question the word order is subject + verb, there is no do/does/did, and there is no question mark.
pairs.whyMn: Дамжуулсан асуултад үгийн дараалал 'эзэн + үйл үг' байна; do/does/did хэрэглэхгүй, асуултын тэмдэг тавихгүй.

pairs.a: 'Are you coming to the party?' he asked.
pairs.b: He asked if I was coming to the party.

pairs.whyMn: Тийм/үгүй асуултыг дамжуулахдаа 'if' эсвэл 'whether' заавал хэрэглэнэ.

pairs.why: Requests and commands become ask/tell + person + to + verb.

mistakes.whyMn: Дамжуулсан асуултад хүүрнэх өгүүлбэрийн үгийн дараалал хэрэглэж, 'did' туслах үйл үгийг хасна.

mistakes.whyMn: Тийм/үгүй асуултыг if/whether + хүүрнэх дараалалтай дамжуулж, цагийг нэг алхам ухраана.

mistakes.wrong: My boss told me don't be late.
mistakes.right: My boss told me not to be late.
mistakes.whyMn: Үгүйсгэсэн тушаал 'not to + үйл үг' хэлбэрт шилжинэ.

mistakes.wrong: She asked me that I was free.
mistakes.right: She asked me if I was free.
mistakes.why: Don't use 'that' after 'ask'. Use if/whether or a question word.
mistakes.whyMn: 'Ask'-ийн дараа 'that' хэрэглэдэггүй; if/whether эсвэл асуух үг хэрэглэнэ.

grammar.title: say vs tell
grammar.summary: Use 'tell' with a person as the object (tell me, tell Anna). Use 'say' without a person, or with 'to + person'. Some fixed expressions always use one verb: tell the truth / a lie / a story / a joke, but say hello / goodbye / sorry / thank you / yes / no.
grammar.summaryMn: 'Tell'-ийн дараа хүн (tell me, tell Anna) заавал орно. 'Say'-ийн дараа хүн шууд орохгүй, хэрэв орвол 'to + хүн' хэлбэртэй. Монгол хэлэнд хоёулаа 'хэлэх' гэж орчуулагддаг тул андуурах нь элбэг. Тогтвортой хэллэгүүдийг цээжлээрэй: tell the truth / a lie / a story / a joke; say hello / goodbye / sorry / thank you.
structure: say + (that) + clause → She said (that) she was tired.
say + something + to + person → He said something to me. · What did she say to you?
tell + person + (that) + clause → She told me (that) she was tired.
tell + person + (not) to + verb → He told us to wait. · She told me not to worry.
tell + person + about + something → Tell me about your trip.
Fixed: tell the truth / a lie / a story / a joke / the time / the difference · say hello / goodbye / sorry / thank you / yes / no

pronunciation.title: Intonation in direct and reported questions
pronunciation.explanation: Questions in English usually have one of two tunes. Yes/no questions (Did you…? Are you…?) often go up ↗ at the end. Wh- questions (Where…? Why…? What…?) usually go down ↘. When you report a question (She asked if…, He wanted to know why…), it is no longer a real question — it is a statement, so your voice goes down ↘ and you don't write a question mark.
pronunciation.explanationMn: Англи асуулт ихэвчлэн хоёр янзын аялгатай. Тийм/үгүй асуулт (Did you…? Are you…?) төгсгөлдөө дээшилдэг ↗. Асуух үгтэй асуулт (Where…? Why…? What…?) ихэвчлэн доошилдог ↘. Асуултыг дамжуулахад (She asked if…, He wanted to know why…) энэ нь жинхэнэ асуулт биш, хүүрнэх өгүүлбэр болно — тиймээс дуу доошилж ↘, асуултын тэмдэг тавихгүй.

vocabulary.definition: a situation in which someone does not understand something correctly
examples: There must be a misunderstanding — I never said I was angry.
Most arguments in our team start with a simple misunderstanding.
vocabulary.mistake: The noun is 'misunderstanding'; the verb is 'misunderstand' (past: misunderstood). Say 'I misunderstood you', not 'I misunderstanding you'.

vocabulary.definition: the feeling or attitude that a voice or a piece of writing expresses
examples: I didn't like the tone of her email — it sounded quite cold.
He said 'fine', but his tone of voice told me he wasn't happy.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'in a friendly tone' (with 'in'), not 'with a friendly tone' or 'by a friendly tone'.
vocabulary.note: In writing, tone comes from word choice and punctuation: 'Fine.' sounds colder than 'Fine, no problem!'

vocabulary.definition: to understand something wrongly, especially someone's words or actions
examples: She misinterpreted my silence as anger.
Short messages are very easy to misinterpret.
vocabulary.mistake: Use 'misinterpret something AS something': 'He misinterpreted my joke as criticism', not 'like criticism'.

vocabulary.definition: to make other people understand what you mean
vocabulary.mn: санаагаа ойлгуулах, хэлэх гэсэн зүйлээ ойлгуулж чадах
examples: It's hard to get your point across in a short text message.
A simple diagram can help you get your point across.
collocations: struggle to get your point across
get your point across in a meeting
vocabulary.note: Change the possessive to match the person: get my / his / her / our point across.

vocabulary.definition: the way you move your body, face and hands, which shows what you are feeling
examples: His body language showed that he was nervous.
In a video call it's harder to read people's body language.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Body language' is uncountable: 'Her body language was friendly', not 'Her body languages were friendly'.

vocabulary.definition: meeting in the same place, not by phone or online
examples: Some problems are much easier to solve face to face.
We've chatted online for months, but we've never met face to face.
vocabulary.note: Before a noun, use hyphens: a face-to-face meeting.

vocabulary.definition: saying what you think directly, without trying to be polite
examples: Her reply was so blunt that I thought she was angry.
To be blunt, your presentation was too long.
vocabulary.note: 'Direct' is often positive; 'blunt' suggests the words felt a little rude.

vocabulary.definition: saying the opposite of what you mean, as a joke or to criticise someone
examples: When he said 'Great job!', I couldn't tell if he was being sarcastic.
Sarcastic comments rarely work well in emails.
vocabulary.mistake: The stress is on the second syllable: sar-CAS-tic, not SAR-cas-tic.

vocabulary.definition: to make something clearer or easier to understand, often by explaining it again
examples: Could you clarify what you mean by 'soon'?
I sent a second email to clarify the meeting time.
vocabulary.mistake: Don't add 'about': 'Can you clarify this?', not 'Can you clarify about this?'
vocabulary.note: Neutral to formal. In conversation you can also say 'Just to be clear, …'

vocabulary.definition: to think that something is true without having proof
examples: I assumed you were busy because you didn't reply.
Don't assume that everyone reads their messages immediately.
vocabulary.mistake: 'Assume' doesn't mean 'check' or 'make sure'. 'I assumed he knew' = I thought he knew, but I didn't check.

vocabulary.definition: to reply, or to react to something
examples: She still hasn't responded to my message.
It's better not to respond when you're angry.
vocabulary.mistake: Say 'respond TO an email', not 'respond an email'.
vocabulary.note: A little more formal than 'reply' or 'get back to someone'.

vocabulary.definition: to think about something too much, so that it becomes worrying or confusing
vocabulary.mn: хэт их бодох, юмыг хэтэрхий бодож санаа зовох
examples: You're overthinking it — she probably just forgot to reply.
I tend to overthink every email I send to my boss.
vocabulary.note: Informal to neutral. Past form: overthought.

reading.title: Lost in Translation: Why Online Messages Go Wrong
text: You send a colleague a quick reply: 'Fine. See you tomorrow.' To you, it is a perfectly friendly message. To your colleague, it sounds cold, maybe even angry. An hour later, they ask if everything is OK, and you have no idea what they are talking about. Situations like this are so common that communication researchers have a name for them: digital misunderstandings.

The main problem is that written messages lose most of the information we normally use to understand each other. When we talk face to face, we hear the other person's tone of voice and see their body language. A smile tells us that a comment is a joke; a raised eyebrow warns us that the speaker is being sarcastic. In a text message, all of that disappears, and the reader has to guess.

Unfortunately, we are not very good at guessing. In one well-known American study, people who sent emails believed that their readers would identify the tone correctly almost 80 per cent of the time. In reality, the readers got it right only a little over half the time. Other research suggests that when we are unsure, we often assume the worst. A short reply seems blunt, and a slow reply looks like a sign that the other person is annoyed.

Age can make things even more complicated. Many younger people read a full stop at the end of a short message as a sign of anger, while their parents simply see correct punctuation. Emojis cause similar problems: a thumbs-up can mean 'Great!' to one person and 'I don't want to talk to you' to another. As a result, different generations regularly misinterpret each other.

So how can we get our point across more clearly? Experts suggest a few simple rules. First, if a topic is important or emotional, don't type it — call or meet in person. Second, read your message again before you send it and ask yourself how it might sound to someone who is tired or stressed. Finally, if a message upsets you, don't respond immediately. Ask the sender to clarify what they meant. Most of the time, you will discover that you were overthinking it — and that 'Fine' really did mean fine.

vocabulary.definition: to move text or images up or down on a screen to see more

vocabulary.definition: a message on your phone or computer that tells you something new has happened

vocabulary.definition: the list of new posts you see when you open a social media app

vocabulary.definition: the videos, texts, photos, etc. that people create and share online

speaking.prompt: Tell the story of a post, video or message that caused a surprise or a small problem — for you or for someone you know. Report what people said, asked and told each other to do.

listening.title: A whole week offline
listening.context: Priya has just come back to work after a week without social media. Her colleague Dan wants to hear about it.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: Priya! Welcome back. So how was it? A whole week offline?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Well, not completely offline. I still had to use email for work. But no social media at all — I deleted the apps on Sunday night.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: Wow. I don't think I could do that. I check my feed about fifty times a day.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: That's exactly why I did it. My screen time was over five hours a day, and I kept picking up my phone without even thinking. To be honest, it was starting to feel a bit addictive.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: So what was the hardest part?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: The first two days, definitely. I had terrible FOMO. My sister told me I was being dramatic, but I honestly felt like everyone was having fun without me.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: Ha! And after that?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: After that it got much easier. I read two novels, I went to bed earlier, and I actually managed to switch off in the evenings.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: Did anyone get annoyed because you weren't replying?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: A couple of people. My friend Jess sent me an email asking if I was angry with her! I had to explain that I'd just gone offline for a week.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: That's funny. So, are you going back to normal now?

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Not exactly. I've put the apps back on, but I've muted most of the group chats and unfollowed about two hundred accounts. I only want to keep up with people I actually care about.

lines.speaker: Dan
lines.text: Hmm, that makes sense. Maybe I should try it — even just for a weekend.

lines.speaker: Priya
lines.text: Honestly, do it. I realised the biggest distraction in my life was sitting in my pocket.

reading.title: Please Don't Call Me: The Rise of Phone Anxiety
text: When Lucy Harding's phone rings, her heart starts to race. 'If it's a number I don't know, I just let it ring,' says the 24-year-old marketing assistant from Manchester. 'Then I search for the number online, and if it's important, I reply by text.' Lucy is far from alone. In one recent British survey, about a quarter of 18- to 34-year-olds said they never answer phone calls, and more than half said they would assume an unexpected call meant bad news.

Experts call this 'phone anxiety', and they say it is not surprising. Many people now in their twenties grew up with messaging apps rather than home phones. For them, a text message has clear advantages: you can think before you reply, check your spelling and choose the right tone. A phone call, on the other hand, happens in real time. There is no chance to plan your words, and there may be awkward silences to deal with.

Some older people find this attitude strange, or even rude. 'When I was young, you called someone to show you cared,' says Martin Reyes, 58, a teacher from Madrid. 'Now my students tell me that calling without warning is almost aggressive. They say you should always send a message first to ask if a call is OK.'

However, avoiding calls completely can cause problems, especially at work. Employers say that some young staff are nervous about calling clients, even when a quick conversation would solve a problem faster than ten emails. As a result, a few companies now offer training courses in which employees practise making simple phone calls.

Psychologists suggest a gradual approach for people who want to feel more confident. Start by calling friends or family members you feel comfortable with, then move on to short practical calls, such as booking a table at a restaurant. Writing down two or three notes before a call can also help. 'The more you do it, the less frightening it becomes,' says one therapist. 'And remember — most calls are over in less than three minutes.'

listening.title: The interview that froze
listening.context: Tom tells his friend Grace about an online job interview he had this morning.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: So? How did the interview go? You look a bit stressed.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Honestly, it was a bit of a disaster. Well, not the interview itself — the internet connection.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: Oh no. What happened?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Everything was fine at the start. The manager, Ms Chen, asked me why I wanted to leave my current job, and I think I gave a really good answer.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: OK, so far so good.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Then she asked me to describe a difficult project, and right in the middle of my answer, the video froze. I kept talking for about two minutes before I realised she couldn't hear me.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: No! What did you do?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: I called her on my phone. She was really nice about it, actually. She said it happened all the time and told me not to worry.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: Well, that's good. Did you get to finish your answer?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Yeah, we finished the interview by phone. But without video I couldn't see her face, so I had no idea if she liked my answers.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: I'm sure it went better than you think. Did she say when they'd let you know?

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: She said they'd contact everyone by Friday. Oh, and she asked if I could send her some examples of my work by tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Grace
lines.text: See? That sounds really positive. They wouldn't ask for more if they weren't interested.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: I hope you're right. Next time I'm doing it from the library — their wi-fi is much better than mine!

writing.sample: In my opinion, social media has made us faster communicators, but not always better ones. On the one hand, it helps me keep up with friends all over the world. My cousin lives in Seoul, and we chat almost every day, which would have been impossible twenty years ago. On the other hand, short messages often lead to misunderstandings. A colleague once told me that she had been upset by my one-word reply, 'OK'. She said it had sounded angry, but I had simply been busy. Since then, I've been more careful with my tone. Having said that, I don't think the technology itself is the problem. All in all, if something really matters, we should talk face to face or at least call — it's still the easiest way to get your point across.

Mei: 'Can we have more time for testing?' Aziz to everyone: 'Please send me your comments by Thursday.' Mei: 'I'm worried about the budget.'
speaking.promptMn: Таны менежер хатагтай Харрис өнөө өглөөний багийн хуралд оролцож чадсангүй. Тэмдэглэлээ ашиглан хурал дээр юу болсныг түүнд дамжуулан ярь.
points: Report Aziz's statement
Report Mei's question
Report Aziz's request
Report Mei's worry and add your own comment
speaking.sample: Good morning, Ms Harris. Let me quickly tell you what happened in the meeting. First, Aziz said that the new website would be ready the following week, so we're more or less on schedule. Then Mei asked whether we could have more time for testing, because she thinks there might be some problems with the mobile version. Aziz didn't respond immediately — he said he would think about it. He also asked us to send him our comments by Thursday. Finally, Mei mentioned that she was worried about the budget. As far as I know, nobody has clarified how much money is left, so maybe you could talk to Aziz about that.

questions.prompt: 'I've lost my phone,' Jamal said. → Jamal said he ___ his phone.
'Do you speak Korean?' → She asked me ___ Korean.
'Where is the station?' → A tourist asked me where the station ___.
answers: was
is
questions.explanation: Usually 'was'; 'is' is also possible because the station is still there.
